heroIntro: Under Order 40 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a civil court in Bangladesh may appoint an impartial Court Receiver to take custody of disputed property, collect rents or business profits, and preserve assets whenever it appears 'just and convenient' during a pending partition, partnership, or commercial lawsuit.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: Court Receiver Under Order 40 CPC
points: Governing Statute: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — Order 40 Rules 1 to 5 (Appointment, Remuneration, Duties & Enforcement).
Legal Standard: 'Just and convenient' test — strong prima facie title plus clear risk of waste, dissipation, or misappropriation.
Receiver's Authority: Custody, rent collection, maintenance, and suing/defending with court leave; acts as an officer of the court.
Appeal Right: An order appointing or refusing to appoint a Receiver is directly appealable under Order 43 Rule 1(s) CPC.

sections.h2: When Does a Court Appoint a Receiver Under Order 40 Rule 1 CPC?
sections.content:
Order 40 Rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 authorises any civil court—whether before or after a decree—to appoint a Receiver of any movable or immovable property whenever it appears just and convenient to do so. A Receiver acts as an impartial officer of the court (custodia legis) to safeguard disputed income-generating assets until final judgment.

In Bangladeshi practice, Order 40 petitions arise most frequently in three high-stakes disputes: (1) family partition suits where one co-sharer pockets all commercial building rent while excluding NRB siblings; (2) partnership dissolution suits where a managing partner diverts cashflow; and (3) mortgaged commercial properties where value is deteriorating.

Because appointing a Receiver dispossesses the party in control, courts apply strict judicial caution; consult our corporate & commercial litigation desk or property litigation lawyer to assess whether an injunction or Receiver best fits your case.

sections.h2: Powers, Duties, and Liabilities of a Court Receiver
sections.content:
Under Order 40 Rules 1(1)(d), 3, and 4 CPC, a Receiver holds only the powers expressly conferred by the court's appointment order and remains strictly accountable to the court for every taka collected or spent.

Order 40 RuleScope of ProvisionPractical Legal Effect
Rule 1(1)(d)Powers to bring/defend suits, collect rents, and manage property.Receiver cannot sell or lease long-term without prior written court permission.
Rule 2Remuneration fixed by general or special court order.Usually a percentage of collections or fixed monthly fee paid from estate funds.
Rule 3Security bond, periodic accounts, and payment of balances.Mandatory submission of audited vouchers and deposit of net rent into court treasury.
Rule 4Enforcement of Receiver's personal liability.Court may attach and sell the Receiver's own property for wilful default or loss.

Note that under Order 40 Rule 5, where the property is land paying revenue to the Government, the court may appoint the District Collector as Receiver with the Collector's consent. For related asset-preservation tools, compare Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 CPC.

sections.h2: Who Can Be Appointed and What Happens to Existing Possession?
sections.content:
A court may appoint a neutral practising advocate, a chartered accountant (in complex corporate/partnership matters), or—with both parties' consent—one of the litigants as Receiver on furnishing a security bond. Critically, Order 40 Rule 1(2) CPC protects third parties who are not parties to the suit: the court cannot remove any person from possession or custody of property whom any party to the suit does not have a present right to remove.

This means tenants holding valid leases are not evicted when a Receiver is appointed; instead, they attorn to the Receiver and deposit monthly rent into the Receiver's court-monitored account rather than paying the disputed landlord. If a party or third person interferes with the Receiver's possession without court leave, they commit contempt of court.

Conversely, if an aggrieved party wishes to challenge a Receiver's appointment or refusal, Order 43 Rule 1(s) CPC grants an immediate right of appeal; see our appeal and revision guide and corporate governance resources.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to Apply for a Receiver in Bangladesh
sections.content:
To persuade a civil court to place disputed rental property or a business under a Receiver, present clear documentary proof of waste or exclusion:

  1. Institute the Substantive Suit First: File the partition, partnership dissolution, or title suit; a standalone Order 40 application without a pending suit is not maintainable.
  2. File Verified Order 40 Rule 1 Petition: Detail the exact monthly rental or business revenue at risk, supported by affidavits showing refusal to render accounts, tax default, or structural waste.
  3. Serve Notice & Conduct Show-Cause Hearing: Courts rarely appoint a Receiver ex parte unless emergency asset destruction is imminent; prepare oral and documentary arguments for the contested hearing.
  4. Settle Security Bond & Terms of Reference: Once allowed, propose a neutral advocate or accountant and ensure the court order specifies rent collection, utility payment, and quarterly accounting dates under Rule 3.
  5. Monitor Quarterly Accounts & Disbursements: Review the Receiver's submitted accounts and apply for interim maintenance or decree-stage distribution; Advocate Md. Shah Alam handles Receiver supervision and appeals before the District Judge and High Court Division.

sections.h2: Documents Checklist for an Order 40 Receiver Petition
sections.content:
Assemble these records to prove both a strong prima facie right and urgent risk of dissipation:

  • Registered title deeds, partition/inheritance records (Warish Certificate), or Partnership Deed establishing your ownership/share.
  • Copies of existing tenant lease agreements, rent receipts, or commercial bank statements showing income generated by the property.
  • Evidence of mismanagement or exclusion (e.g., unpaid utility/municipal bills, refusal letters, or bank diversion records).
  • Schedule of all properties, shops, or accounts to be placed under the Receiver's management.
  • Legal notices demanding accounts and, for NRBs abroad, an Embassy-attested Power of Attorney.

faqs.question: Can a Court Receiver be appointed in a family partition suit in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. In partition suits where one co-sharer is in exclusive possession of a multi-storied building or market collecting substantial rent while refusing to share accounts or income with other heirs, courts frequently appoint a Receiver under Order 40 Rule 1 CPC to collect and deposit rent in court.

faqs.question: Can a person sue a Court Receiver without permission of the court?
faqs.answer: No. Because a Receiver is an officer of the court holding property in custodia legis, no suit or legal proceeding can be instituted against a Receiver in respect of the managed property without first obtaining leave (permission) of the appointing court.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Court Receiver and a Temporary Injunction?
faqs.answer: A Temporary Injunction (Order 39) restrains a party from selling or altering property while leaving them in possession. A Court Receiver (Order 40) removes management and rent collection from the parties altogether and places the asset under neutral court custody.

faqs.question: Can a Receiver sell disputed property during the lawsuit?
faqs.answer: A Receiver has no inherent power to sell immovable property. However, if perishable goods or depreciating assets are involved, or all parties consent, the court may expressly authorise a sale under Order 40 Rule 1(1)(d) subject to court confirmation.

faqs.question: Can an order appointing a Receiver be appealed in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Order 43 Rule 1(s) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, an order appointing or refusing to appoint a Receiver under Order 40 Rule 1 is directly appealable to the appellate court (District Judge or High Court Division depending on suit valuation).
